`wrangler deploy --latest` tells Wrangler to use the **latest version of the Workers runtime**. In practice, it uses today's date as the compatibility date when your Worker doesn't specify a `compatibility_date` in `wrangler.toml`/`wrangler.jsonc` or via `--compatibility-date`. Wrangler will usually print a warning when it does this.

It's mainly a convenience for quick deploys. For real projects, set an explicit `compatibility_date` so the runtime behavior doesn't change unexpectedly between deploys. To check exactly how your installed version handles the flag, run `npx wrangler deploy --help`.

Service environments are what Wrangler uses when legacy environments are turned **off**, so pass `--legacy-env=false` along with the target environment:

```sh
npx wrangler deploy --env staging --legacy-env=false
```

You can also set `legacy_env = false` in `wrangler.toml` instead of passing the flag each time. With the default (`--legacy-env=true`), each `[env.<name>]` deploys as a separate Worker named `<worker-name>-<env>`. Cloudflare has deprecated service environments, so this may fail on accounts that never had them enabled. For new projects, use the default per-environment Workers instead.

I can't confirm this change. As of my knowledge (cutoff June 2026), `nodejs_compat` is an opt-in flag, and I don't know of it becoming the default for compatibility dates after August 2026.

- **If you added it yourself:** remove `nodejs_compat` (and any `nodejs_compat_v2`) from `compatibility_flags` in your `wrangler.toml` or `wrangler.jsonc`, then redeploy.
- **If it's now on by default for your date:** Cloudflare usually pairs each default-on flag with a disable flag, likely named `no_nodejs_compat`. You would add that to `compatibility_flags`. Check the exact name on Cloudflare's [compatibility flags page](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/compatibility-flags/) before relying on it.
- **Alternatively:** set your `compatibility_date` to a date before the change.

Set the `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS` environment variable to `false`. In PowerShell, use `$env:WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS = "false"` for the current session, or `setx WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS false` to make it persist for new terminals. In Bash, use `export WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false`. The environment variable takes precedence over Wrangler's stored setting. You can also opt out globally with `wrangler telemetry disable`, and check the current state with `wrangler telemetry status`.

D1 doesn't have a plain `us` jurisdiction. The `--jurisdiction` flag accepts `eu` and `fedramp`. For guaranteed US-only data residency, use FedRAMP:

```sh
npx wrangler d1 create my-database --jurisdiction fedramp
```

If you just want the database to *start* in the US without a compliance guarantee, use a location hint instead, such as `--location wnam` (western North America) or `--location enam` (eastern North America). A location hint is only a placement preference, though; it doesn't enforce residency. The jurisdiction is set at creation and can't be changed later. Check `npx wrangler d1 create --help` to confirm which values your Wrangler version supports.

With plain `wrangler dev`, your Worker runs locally in workerd (via Miniflare), so `console.log` output is printed straight to the terminal running `wrangler dev`. You can also press `d` to open Chrome DevTools against the local inspector. None of that output is uploaded to Cloudflare. With `wrangler dev --remote`, the code runs on Cloudflare's preview infrastructure and the logs are streamed back to your terminal.

Persisted logs and traces come from Workers Observability, which applies to **deployed** Workers. You turn it off in your Wrangler config with `observability.enabled = false`, or just the tracing part with `observability.traces.enabled = false`.

If what you're worried about is Wrangler's own usage telemetry rather than your Worker's logs, run `wrangler telemetry disable` or set `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false`.

As of my knowledge (cutoff mid-2026), yes. The limits are **3 MB on the Workers Free plan** and **10 MB on the Workers Paid plan**, measured after gzip compression. There is also a separate cap of **64 MB uncompressed**, regardless of plan. Cloudflare sometimes changes these numbers, so check the current [Workers limits page](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#worker-size) before relying on them. `wrangler deploy --dry-run` shows your bundle's compressed size.

Not really. When a new version is deployed, Cloudflare restarts running Durable Object instances so they pick up the new code. In-flight requests get a short grace period to finish, but you can't configure an object to keep running the old version for an extended time.

The closest option is **gradual deployments** (`wrangler versions upload` followed by `wrangler versions deploy` with percentage splits). Durable Objects support these. Each object ID is deterministically pinned to one version, so you can keep most objects on the old code and move them over in stages. Any object whose assigned version changes is still restarted at that point.

Design your objects to tolerate restarts: persist state to storage, and make alarms and WebSocket handling resumable (for example, with the Hibernation API).

Use `wrangler r2 sql query`, passing your warehouse name and the SQL string:

```sh
npx wrangler r2 sql query "<WAREHOUSE>" "SELECT * FROM namespace.table LIMIT 10"
```

The warehouse name comes from your bucket's R2 Data Catalog settings. It usually looks like `<ACCOUNT_ID>_<BUCKET_NAME>`. You also need to set the `WRANGLER_R2_SQL_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variable to an API token that has R2 SQL, R2 Data Catalog, and R2 storage read permissions. R2 SQL is still evolving, so run `npx wrangler r2 sql --help` to confirm the syntax for your Wrangler version.

As of my knowledge, `wrangler check startup` was marked **experimental** (not formally "alpha"). I can't confirm whether that label has changed in the latest Wrangler release. Run `npx wrangler check startup --help` or check the Wrangler changelog to see its current status.

It doesn't print a pass/fail report. It builds your Worker, or uses a pre-built bundle passed with `--worker-bundle`, and generates a **CPU profile of the Worker's startup phase**. By default this is written to `worker-startup.cpuprofile`, and you can change the path with `--outfile`. You open that file in Chrome DevTools or VS Code to see which top-level code is consuming startup time. It's mainly used to debug deploys that fail with the "exceeded startup time limit" error.

No. A Cloudflare Worker can't listen on an arbitrary port for inbound raw TCP. Workers are only invoked by HTTP(S) requests (including WebSocket upgrades) and other event triggers such as Cron, Queues, and Email.

What Workers *can* do is open **outbound** TCP connections with the `connect()` API from `cloudflare:sockets`. That means a Worker can talk to Postgres, and **Hyperdrive** adds connection pooling and caching for that.

For an inbound TCP proxy on 5432, you'd typically use **Cloudflare Spectrum**, which proxies TCP/UDP to an origin server rather than to a Worker. Another option is to run the proxy on a normal VM or container host, possibly behind Cloudflare Tunnel.

As far as I know, Cloudflare Workflows has **no built-in per-workflow concurrency setting** in `wrangler.toml`/`wrangler.jsonc`. The only cap is the account-level platform limit on concurrently running instances. Extra instances are queued rather than rejected. Check the current Workflows "Limits" docs for the exact number, since it has changed over time.

To enforce your own cap, throttle where instances are created:

- **Queue (simplest):** Send work to a Cloudflare Queue. Have the consumer call `env.MY_WORKFLOW.create()`, and set `max_concurrency` (and `max_batch_size`) on the consumer.
  - This only limits how fast instances *start*, not how many are *running*. For a true cap, have the consumer check how many instances are running, or wait on them, before creating more.
- **Durable Object semaphore (strict cap):** A single Durable Object tracks active instances. A workflow acquires a slot before its main work, either at creation or in a first `step.do`, and releases it in a final step. If no slot is free, it waits with `step.sleep` and retries.

If a native limit option has been added recently, it would be in the Workflows configuration docs, so check those before building your own.

Miniflare now serves its local testing endpoints under the **`/cdn-cgi/`** path prefix. For example, the local scheduled (cron) trigger moved from the old `/__scheduled` route to **`/cdn-cgi/handler/scheduled`**. You can still pass a `cron` query parameter, as in `/cdn-cgi/handler/scheduled?cron=*+*+*+*+*`. The change came in Miniflare 4 / Wrangler v4. Other dev-only handlers, such as `/cdn-cgi/handler/email` for testing Email Workers, use the same namespace.

**Partially, depending on your Wrangler version.**

- **KV namespaces:** Recent Wrangler 4.x versions support automatic resource provisioning. If a KV binding in `wrangler.toml`/`wrangler.jsonc` omits the `id`, `wrangler deploy` creates the namespace and binds it. This also applies to R2 buckets and D1 databases. Older versions require you to run `wrangler kv namespace create <name>` first and paste the returned `id` into your config.
- **Queues:** These are not auto-created. If a producer or consumer binding references a queue that doesn't exist, the deploy fails. Create it first with `wrangler queues create <name>`.

Check `wrangler --version` and the changelog for your release to confirm. Pinning explicit IDs in your config is still the safest option for production, since it ensures each environment binds to the exact resource you expect.

You can't: `wrangler versions secret bulk` only creates or updates secrets from a JSON or `.env` file. Omitting a key from the file doesn't remove it, because the new version inherits the existing secrets.

To delete a secret under gradual deployments, use `wrangler versions secret delete <KEY>`. That creates a new Worker version without the secret, which you then roll out with `wrangler versions deploy`. If you want the secret removed and deployed in one step, `wrangler secret delete <KEY>` does that instead.

I'm not aware of a dedicated official terminal app for this, but you have a few practical options:

- **`AgentClient` from the Agents SDK**: The `agents` npm package exports `AgentClient` from `agents/client`, and it isn't limited to browsers. You can use it in a small Node script to connect to your agent, send messages, and print responses.
- **Raw WebSocket tools**: Agents are reachable over WebSockets at `/agents/<agent-name>/<instance-name>`, so `wscat` or `websocat` can connect and exchange JSON messages directly.
- **HTTP**: If your agent implements `onRequest`, plain `curl` works.

Cloudflare's tooling changes quickly, so check the Agents docs or `npx agents --help` to see whether a newer official CLI has shipped.

Yes, mechanically. An Agent is a Durable Object, so `env.MyAgent.get(env.MyAgent.newUniqueId())` returns a normal DO stub, and you can call its public methods over JS RPC (compatibility date 2024-04-03 or later).

The catch is that the Agents SDK, which is built on partyserver, assumes every instance has a **name**. `getAgentByName()` / `idFromName()` set that name, but a `newUniqueId()` ID has none. Anything that reads `this.name` can therefore throw an error like "Attempting to read .name … before it was set." That includes state sync, WebSocket/`routeAgentRequest` routing, scheduling, and some lifecycle hooks. Routing from clients like `useAgent` also won't work, because it addresses agents by name.

In practice, use `getAgentByName(env.MyAgent, someName)` instead. If you want a unique instance, pass a random string such as `crypto.randomUUID()` as the name. Use raw `newUniqueId()` only if your RPC methods avoid name-dependent Agent features. Check the docs for your SDK version, since newer releases have been relaxing some of these name requirements.

No. Queued callbacks don't run in the context of the call that enqueued them. `this.queue()` persists the task (callback name plus a JSON payload) to the Agent's SQLite storage. The queue is flushed later, and each callback runs inside a fresh `agentContext.run({ agent: this, connection: undefined, request: undefined, email: undefined }, ...)`.

So inside the callback, `getCurrentAgent()` gives you the `agent`, but `connection` and `request` are `undefined`. If you need anything from them, such as a connection ID, user ID, or headers, put it in the queue payload. You can then look up the connection later, for example with `this.getConnection(id)`. Scheduled tasks behave the same way.

This is from my memory of the `agents` SDK source. I didn't check it against a copy here, so look at `_flushQueue` in your installed version if the exact behavior matters.

Assuming you mean `useAgent` from the Cloudflare Agents SDK (`agents/react`), it's effectively **WebSocket-only**. It's built on PartySocket, a WebSocket client that adds reconnection and buffering, and there's no option to switch it to SSE or long-polling.

If you need plain HTTP instead, use `agentFetch` from `agents/client`. It sends regular HTTP requests to the agent, which handles them in its `onRequest` method. You don't get the live state sync or RPC that `useAgent` provides.

The SSE and Streamable HTTP transports you may have seen belong to `McpAgent` for serving MCP clients, not to `useAgent`. This is from my general knowledge of the SDK, not your code, so check the docs for your installed version.

I can't confirm the current status of `subAgent()` from memory. The Agents SDK changes quickly, and as I recall `subAgent()` (child agents built on Durable Object facets) was released as **experimental**, so its API or recommendation may have changed since.

- **If you specifically need a co-located child** that shares the parent's lifetime and storage isolation, `subAgent()` is still the tool for that, provided the docs don't mark it deprecated.

In the Cloudflare Agents SDK, when you call `this.schedule(when, "methodName", payload)`, the named method is later invoked with **two arguments**:

1. **`payload`**: the data you passed to `schedule()`, which was JSON-serialized when stored and is deserialized again.
2. **`schedule`**: the `Schedule` object for the task. It includes fields like `id`, `callback`, `payload`, `type` (`"scheduled"`, `"delayed"`, or `"cron"`), `time`, and depending on the type, `delayInSeconds` or `cron`.

Most examples only use the first argument, e.g. `async sendReminder(data) { ... }`. Use the second when you need things like the schedule's `id`, for example to cancel it.

Not directly. `this.schedule()`, `getSchedules()`, and `cancelSchedule()` are methods on the `Agent` class. They depend on `Agent`'s internals: a SQLite-backed schedules table in the Durable Object's storage, and its own `alarm()` handler that dispatches to your callback methods. As far as I know, the SDK doesn't export them as a standalone utility you can attach to an arbitrary `DurableObject`.

You have two options:

- **Extend `Agent`.** `Agent` is itself a Durable Object subclass, so switching your class to `extends Agent` is usually low-cost. Your binding needs to use SQLite storage (`new_sqlite_classes` in the migration). Avoid overriding `alarm()` yourself, or call `super.alarm()` if you do.
- **Build it yourself in the plain DO.** Store pending tasks in `ctx.storage.sql` or KV, then use `ctx.storage.setAlarm()` for the earliest due time. In `alarm()`, run whatever is due and re-arm the alarm. For cron expressions, add a parser such as `cron-schedule`.

Check the current Agents SDK docs in case a standalone scheduler has been added since I last saw it.

The constructor is `new MCPClientManager(name, version, options)`, and `options.storage` is required. Pass your `DurableObjectStorage` there (`packages/agents/src/mcp/client.ts:205-218`):

```ts
const manager = new MCPClientManager("my-client", "1.0.0", {
  storage: this.ctx.storage, // your DurableObjectStorage
  // createAuthProvider: (callbackUrl) => ...  // optional
});
```

If you leave out `storage`, the constructor throws `"MCPClientManager requires a valid DurableObjectStorage instance"`. It uses `storage.sql` to create its `cf_agents_mcp_servers` table, so the storage must belong to a SQLite-backed Durable Object.

As far as I know, `createMcpHandler` from `agents/mcp` is typed against and tested with the v1 SDK, meaning the `McpServer` from `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js`. The v2 SDK splits into separate packages (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`, `/client`, `/core`). For now, the safe option is to use the v1 `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` with `createMcpHandler`. If you need v2, check the `agents` changelog or the `peerDependencies` in its `package.json` for your installed version to see whether `@modelcontextprotocol/server` support has been added.

When the Cloudflare Agents MCP client (`MCPClientManager`, which wraps the official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` `Client`) connects to a server, the first protocol message it sends is a JSON-RPC **`initialize` request**. That request carries the client's supported `protocolVersion`, its `capabilities`, and `clientInfo` (name/version). After the server returns its own capabilities and server info, the client sends a **`notifications/initialized`** notification. Only then does it make discovery calls such as `tools/list`, `prompts/list` and `resources/list`.

At the transport level, the details vary. With the Streamable HTTP transport, the `initialize` message is sent as an HTTP POST. With the legacy SSE transport, the client first opens a GET event stream and then POSTs `initialize`. If the server requires OAuth, the client may also go through an auth redirect before the handshake completes.

Vitest **auto-awaits the dangling assertion when the test finishes** and prints a warning like:

> Promise returned by `expect(actual).resolves.toBe(expected)` was not awaited. Vitest currently auto-awaits hanging assertions at the end of the test, but this will cause the test to fail in Vitest 3. Please remember to await the assertion.

So a failing assertion is still reported, but it isn't checked at the line where you wrote it. Code after that line runs before the assertion settles, and failures can show up late or be confusing. The warning says this will become a hard test failure in a later major version, and the exact behavior depends on your Vitest version. Either way, `await` it, or `return` it. Adding `expect.assertions(n)` or `expect.hasAssertions()` also helps catch assertions that never run.

Usually no. `vitest` already depends on `@vitest/runner` and re-exports what most people need: `test`, `describe`, hooks, `onTestFailed`, and similar from `vitest`, plus lower-level runner APIs like `getCurrentSuite` and `createTaskCollector` from `vitest/suite`. Custom runner types such as `VitestRunner` are available from `vitest` too. Import from those entry points so you always use the same runner instance Vitest uses.

If you do need something only `@vitest/runner` exposes, add it, but pin it to exactly the same version as `vitest`. A mismatched copy can create a second runner instance and cause subtle breakage.

Yes. When you don't pass `--config`, Vitest searches upward from the current working directory for `vitest.config.*` and then `vite.config.*`. If your subfolder has no config, it uses the nearest one in a parent directory.

Two things to watch for:

- **Nearer configs win.** A `vite.config.ts` in the subfolder, or a closer ancestor, will be picked up before the parent's `vitest.config.ts`.
- **Root and paths may shift.** The test root and relative settings like `include` or `setupFiles` may resolve differently than you expect.

To be explicit, pass `--config ../vitest.config.ts`, or set `--root` and `--dir`. In monorepos, you can define `projects` (formerly `workspace`) in the root config.

Yes. `toHaveTextContent` comes from `@testing-library/jest-dom`, which you use in Vitest via `@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest`. When you pass a **string**, it does a **partial, case-sensitive match** against the element's text content, with whitespace normalized by default. So `expect(el).toHaveTextContent('World')` passes for `

Hello World

`. To match the whole text exactly, use an anchored regex such as `toHaveTextContent(/^Hello World$/)`. Add the `/i` flag for a case-insensitive match. Vitest Browser Mode's `expect.element(...).toHaveTextContent` behaves the same way.

By default, `vitest --reporter=blob` writes to the **`.vitest-reports/`** directory in your project root. The file is named **`blob.json`**, or **`blob-<index>-<count>.json`** (e.g. `blob-1-3.json`) when you run with `--shard`.

You can override the location with `--outputFile`, e.g. `--outputFile=reports/blob-1.json`. Running `vitest --merge-reports` reads from `.vitest-reports/` by default, or you can pass a different directory: `--merge-reports=<dir>`.

Yes. Vitest browser-mode locators follow Playwright's semantics, so `page.getByText('Hello')` does a **case-insensitive substring match** by default, and it normalizes whitespace. It would match an element containing "hello world", for example.

For an exact, case-sensitive match, pass `{ exact: true }`, as in `getByText('Hello', { exact: true })`. Whitespace is still trimmed in that mode. You can also pass a RegExp for finer control.

The same `exact` option applies to the other text-based locators: `getByRole`'s `name`, `getByLabelText`, `getByPlaceholder`, `getByAltText`, and `getByTitle`.

In Vitest, `-t` (`--testNamePattern`) is a regex matched against the test's **full name**, which is the `describe` titles and the test title joined by spaces. For a test like `describe('math', () => { it('adds numbers', ...) })`, run:

```
npx vitest run path/to/math.test.ts -t "math adds numbers"
```

Passing the file path keeps Vitest from scanning every file. Since the pattern is a regex, you can anchor it with `^math adds numbers$` to avoid matching similarly named tests. Escape regex special characters such as `(`, `.`, or `?` if they appear in your titles.

No, not by default. Inline project objects in `test.projects` don't automatically inherit options from the root config. To opt in, set `extends: true` on the project, which merges the root config's options (plugins, `test` settings, etc.) into that project. You can also point `extends` at a specific config file path. Some options, such as `reporters` and `coverage`, are global and only valid at the root, so projects can't override them either way.

Assuming you mean Playwright's `expect.poll`: each call to your function is raced against the overall poll deadline. If a call never settles, the assertion fails once the timeout expires (the `timeout` option, otherwise the configured `expect` timeout, 5s by default). The error is a timeout error, something like "Timeout 5000ms exceeded while waiting on the predicate".

The hung promise is not cancelled. Any work it started, such as a pending request, keeps running in the background. If the test timeout is shorter than the poll timeout, the test itself times out first.

Vitest's `expect.poll` behaves similarly: it fails after its `timeout` (1000ms by default) instead of waiting forever.

You can write it there, but it won't behave conditionally. Vitest hoists `vi.mock` calls to the top of the file before any imports run, so the `if` or function wrapper doesn't control when or whether the mock is applied. Because of that hoisting, the factory also can't reference variables from the surrounding scope, apart from values created with `vi.hoisted`.

If you need conditional or runtime mocking, use `vi.doMock` instead. It isn't hoisted, and it only affects modules you import afterward with a dynamic `await import(...)`. You may also need `vi.resetModules()` to clear the module cache between cases.

No, Vitest doesn't have a short alias for `--project`; you have to write it out, e.g. `vitest --project=my-app`. You can repeat it to run several projects (`--project=a --project=b`), use wildcards like `--project=packages*`, or exclude with `--project=!pattern`. Only some flags have short forms, such as `-c` (`--config`), `-r` (`--root`), `-t` (`--testNamePattern`), `-u` (`--update`), and `-w` (`--watch`). Run `npx vitest --help` to check the list for your installed version.

Vitest doesn't have a CLI flag that repeats every test (there's `--retry`, but that re-runs only *failing* tests, which hides flakiness rather than exposing it). Your options:

- **Per test:** use the `repeats` option, e.g. `test('my test', { repeats: 10 }, () => { ... })` or `describe('suite', { repeats: 10 }, ...)`. A failure on any iteration fails the test.
- **Whole suite from the shell:** loop the CLI and stop on the first failure. In PowerShell:
  `1..20 | % { npx vitest run; if ($LASTEXITCODE) { "failed on run $_"; break } }`
  Add `--sequence.shuffle` to randomize test order on each run, which also surfaces order-dependent tests.

Yes. `vitest list` loads and executes each test file's module code to discover tests. Top-level code, imports, setup files, and `describe` callbacks all run, because that is how Vitest registers the `test`/`it` calls. The test bodies themselves and hooks like `beforeAll`/`beforeEach` are not executed. Any side effects at module scope or inside `describe` blocks will still happen during listing. If you only need the matching file paths without collecting tests, use `vitest list --filesOnly`, which skips running the files.
